prior_authoring.short_description: H.R.1 Senate replacement: selected border, detention and asylum, employment-authorization and selected sponsor/enforcement fees
prior_authoring.compact_description: Selected Senate H.R. 1 provisions would fund border infrastructure and detention, set fiscal 2025 asylum filing/pending fee floors of $100 each and specified asylum/parole/TPS employment-authorization initial/renewal fee floors of $550/$275, with distinct duration and termination rules. This is a whole-replacement concurrence choice, with qualifications.
prior_authoring.meaning:
This July3 House concurrence concerns the Senate's July1 EAS, which strikes all after the first word and replaces the earlier H.R.1 text. It is the complete multi-domain reconciliation replacement, not a second passage of the unchanged House bill or a separate vote on its Immigration components. Selected Immigration highlights here concern border infrastructure, detention and asylum fees; other immigration-related benefits, taxes, employment authorization, child-sponsor, reimbursement and enforcement provisions are not exhaustively described. Section90001 would appropriate an additional $46.55billion for fiscal2025 to CBP, available until September30,2029, for new/replacement primary, waterborne and secondary barriers, access roads, detection attributes and ground preparation for CBP operations and barrier construction/maintenance. The different House60001 accounts are not silently used to define this replacement amount or its purposes. Section90003 would appropriate an additional $45billion for fiscal2025 to ICE, available until September30,2029, for single-adult alien detention and family residential-center capacity. Aliens MAY be detained at family centers pending an INA removal decision and, if ordered removed, until removal. Single-adult detention standards are set in the Secretary's discretion CONSISTENT WITH APPLICABLE LAW. The family-center definition covers apprehended/encountered family units, including children who are not statutorily defined unaccompanied alien children, and does not reproduce the House's express regardless-of-State-licensing clause.6USC279(g)(2) requires no lawful immigration status, under18 age, and no US parent/legal guardian or none available for care/physical custody. Neither the capacity funding nor permission establishes automatic detention/removal of every alien, elimination of all legal constraints or actual operations. Section100002 requires an additional fee upon filing an asylum application. The fiscal2025 amount is the greater of $100 or the amount set by DHS/the Attorney General, as applicable, by rule; it cannot be waived/reduced. From fiscal2026 the prior fiscal-year fee is increased by the printed July-to-July CPI-U increment rounded down to a multiple of $10. Half of Attorney-General-filed receipts go to EOIR; half of DHS-filed receipts go to USCIS's existing Immigration Examinations Fee Account, retained/expended without further appropriation; uncredited receipts go to Treasury. This $100 filing floor differs from the House's $1,000 floor. Section100009 separately requires an additional fee for EACH CALENDAR YEAR an asylum application remains pending. Its fiscal2025 amount is the greater of $100 or a DHS rule amount, followed by the printed CPI-U annual adjustment with the increment rounded DOWN TO THE NEAREST DOLLAR; receipts go to Treasury and the fee cannot be waived/reduced. Do not transfer that rounding to the initial-filing fee or back to the House's differently printed yearly formula. Section100018 changes pre-vote INA208(d)(3)/8USC1158(d)(3) from MAY impose fees to SHALL and replaces the following cost-cap/installment/nonmandatory-fee language with preserved additional adjudication/naturalization-fee authority under286(m). The baseline already authorized asylum-consideration, employment-authorization and asylum-based adjustment fees;1356(m)/(n) govern existing account/cost-recovery context. No first-ever fee authority, new asylum eligibility test from that edit, specific implemented collection rule or actual payment is inferred. Employment-authorization fees are separate from asylum filing and annual pending-application fees. Senate100003 requires additional initial application fees for asylum applicants under1158(d)(2), paroled aliens andTPS employment-authorization applicants under1254a(a)(1)(B). Each fiscal2025 floor is$550 or a higher DHS rule amount, with no waiver/reduction and fiscal2026-onward July-to-July CPI-U increments rounded down to$10. The asylum-initial subsection contains no House-style six-month duration sentence; it credits25percent of fees collected PURSUANT TO THIS SUBSECTION to USCIS's existing fee account, retained/expended without further appropriation with NOT LESS THAN50percent of the credited share for benefit-fraud detection/prevention, and sends the rest to Treasury. Parole/TPS initial fees go to Treasury; their initial authorizations last one year or the duration of parole/TPS respectively, whichever is shorter. Senate100010 and100012 set separate parole/TPS employment-authorization renewal/extension fiscal2025 fee floors of$275, possible higher DHS rule amounts and later CPI increments rounded down to$10. Each sends25percent to USCIS's existing fee account to retain/spend without further appropriation and the rest to Treasury; no waiver/reduction.100012 states one year or the duration of the designation ofTPS, whichever is shorter.100010 literally says employment authorization for each paroled alien, OR ANY RENEWAL OR EXTENSION OF SUCH PAROLE, shall be valid for one year or parole duration, whichever is shorter. Preserve this printed antecedent and leave its application unresolved; do not rewrite it into a new parole-eligibility rule or import House six-month text. Senate100011 imposes at least$275 for each asylum-based employment-authorization renewal/extension, with25percent credited to USCIS's existing fee account without further appropriation, the rest to Treasury and no waiver/reduction. It prints no annual CPI formula or House-style six-month limit. It retains the three termination points: immediately after asylum-officer denial unless referred to an immigration judge;30days after immigration-judge denial unless timely appealed to BIA; immediately after BIA denies an appeal of asylum denial. It does not reproduce the separate House70013(d) prohibition on later grants/renewals/extensions absent a FederalCourtOfAppeals remand. Absence of that House sentence does not establish unlimited permission or erase other law. The complete pre-vote1158(d)(2) already permits regulated asylum-based work authorization while denying entitlement and preserving a180day wait for applicants not otherwise eligible. Existing1254a(a)(1)(B)/(a)(2) authorizes employment throughout TPS. Document-validity clauses do not themselves terminate TPS, create first employment authority or establish individual eligibility. Existing1182(d)(5)(A)/(B) preserves case-by-case temporary humanitarian/significant-public-benefit parole subject to the printed statutory exceptions, including its refugee qualification and the distinction from admission; paying a fee does not supply parole or work permission. Senate100016 requires a fiscal2025 fee of at least$5,000, or a higher DHS rule amount, on an alien BOTH ordered removed in absentia under1229a(b)(5) AND subsequently arrested by ICE, with fiscal2026-onward CPI-U increments rounded down to$10. It does not apply if the order was rescinded under1229a(b)(5)(C).50percent goes to ICE's Detention and Removal Office Fee Account, retained/expended without further appropriation; the rest goes to Treasury. It expressly bars waiver/reduction. These fee conditions preserve the underlying notice/address/removability proof, rescission, exceptional-circumstances definition and motion-to-reopen stay in complete pre-vote1229a(b)(5)/(e) and1229(a); an actual order/arrest, new removal ground or denied legal review is not inferred. Senate100017 separately requires an additional fee from any INADMISSIBLE alien at the time the person is apprehended BETWEEN PORTS OF ENTRY. Its fiscal2025 floor is$5,000 or a higher DHS rule amount, with later CPI-U increments rounded down to$10. Unlike House70022, this operative sentence does not name CBP as the apprehending actor. It prints TWO proceeds clauses: subsection(c) sends50percent to ICE's Detention and Removal Office Fee Account for retention/spending without further appropriation and the remainder to Treasury; subsection(d) says ALL fees under the section go to Treasury. The exact EAS HTML and officialPDF pages827-828 both print these clauses. The candidate preserves the apparent allocation conflict and does not choose an operative distribution. No express no-waiver clause is printed in100017; do not import100016(e) or House70022(d), or infer that a waiver is available. These are exact between-port/inadmissibility and in-absentia-plus-ICE-arrest fee predicates, not all enforcement encounters or a fee-imposed finding that an alien actually met any predicate. Senate100004 adds a parole-entry fee with fiscal2025floor$1,000 or higher DHS rule amount, subsequent CPI-U increments rounded down to$10 and Treasury disposition. Its exceptions require the alien to establish the parole reason to DHS's satisfaction on an INDIVIDUAL,CASE-BY-CASE basis; its no-waiver clause expressly preserves those exceptions. The fee exceptions retain their actual predicates: a medical emergency with necessary treatment unavailable in the foreign state where the alien resides OR a life-threatening emergency with insufficient normal-visa time; the parent/legal guardian of such a medical-emergency MINOR; the alien needed in the US to donate an organ or tissue for transplant, with insufficient normal-visa time; a close family member in the United States whose death is imminent, when normal visa processing would prevent arriving while that person is alive; or seeking to attend a close family member's funeral, when normal visa processing would prevent arriving in the United States in time for it; an adopted child's urgent treatment needed before expected final adoption-related visa issuance while in the petitioner's legal custody; a LAWFUL INA245 adjustment applicant returning after temporary travel abroad; and a person returned to a contiguous country under235(b)(2)(C) paroled to attend the person's immigration hearing. The law-enforcement significant-public-benefit exception requires a DHS determination that significant public benefit has resulted or will result from the parole, BOTH assistance to the USGovernment AND presence required in that matter, PLUS at least one of inadmissibility, failure to meet nonimmigrant-admission eligibility, or insufficient normal-visa time; it is not every asserted public benefit. Senate exception9 instead requires that the alien HASBEENGRANTED the status of Cuban/Haitianentrant as defined inPL96-422Sec501(e). That complete definition distinguishes special Cuban/Haitianentrant-parole/subsequently-established special-status categories from OTHERCuban/Haitian nationals with the listed parole/no-other-status, removal-proceeding or pending-asylum alternatives AND no final,nonappealable,legally-enforceable removal order. Its status-at-assistance/services wording is preserved in the bound definition, not silently turned into proof of the fee-specific grant condition or a nationality-only exemption. Do not use the different House Cuba-residence/family-petition/program conjunction to define this replacement, or infer actual parole/fee exemption from nationality. Existing1182(d)(5) authority/statutory exceptions/non-admission distinction remain; paying or excepting a fee does not grant parole, admission or adjustment. Senate100005 requires an additional SIJapplication fee from ANYALIEN,PARENT,ORLEGALGUARDIAN of an alien applying under1101(a)(27)(J), with fiscal2025floor$250 or a higher DHS rule amount, later CPI increments rounded down to$10 and Treasury disposition. It does not print the House one-viable-parent fee predicate or the House express waiver bar; no waiver availability or separate cumulative charges on every named payer are inferred. Complete1101(a)(27)(J) retains the juvenile-court dependency/custody and1ORboth-parent nonviability findings, best-interest-against-return finding, DHSconsent, HHS-specific custody-jurisdiction consent and no derivative parentage rights. These fee provisions do not grant SIJstatus, import a UAC-under18 definition or alter those eligibility findings by themselves. Senate100006 edits EXISTING1254a(c)(1)(B) registration authority: it raises the statutory fee MAXIMUM from$50 to$500, subject to fiscal2026-onward CPI-U adjustments rounded down to$10. It leaves the existing AttorneyGeneral MAYrequire a REASONABLE registration fee language and separate work-document fee authority; this is not a mandatory universal$500charge, a$500minimum, the House conditional additional fee or the separate$550initial/$275renewal EADfees. The amendment adds Treasury disposition and no waiver/reduction of required fees. The existing appropriation-credit sentence is NOTEXPRESSLYSTRUCK in the printed edit and remains in redesignatedclause(i), alongside addedclause(iii) directing all fees under the subparagraph to Treasury. Preserve that apparent proceeds interaction for legal/application review rather than silently deleting the baseline sentence or choosing an implemented distribution. The proposed registration-cap change does not grant or end TPS, guarantee status eligibility, prove payment or establish an individual's outcome. Senate 100007 adds a visa-integrity fee payable by any alien issued a nonimmigrant visa at issuance, in addition to other authorized fees. The fiscal 2025 minimum is $250 or a higher DHS rule amount; subsequent July-to-July CPI-U increments are rounded down to the nearest dollar. Unreimbursed fees go to Treasury and the applicable fee cannot be waived or reduced. DHS MAY reimburse after the visa period of validity expires only if the alien demonstrates compliance with ALL visa conditions after admission, including no unauthorized employment, AND one of two printed alternatives: (A) did not seek to extend the period of admission during the visa validity period AND departed no later than five days after the last day of "such period"; OR (B) during that validity period WAS GRANTED an extension of nonimmigrant status or adjustment to lawful permanent resident status. The text uses "such period" in alternative (A); its application is reserved rather than silently choosing visa validity or authorized admission as the referent. The House nonuse, filing-only and change-of-status alternatives are not imported into this version. A filing is not a grant; reimbursement remains discretionary and conditional, not guaranteed repayment or a general permission to stay/work. The complete pre-vote 1101(a)(26) definition distinguishes proper nonimmigrant visa issuance from actual admission, compliance or an individual outcome. Senate 100008 separately adds an I-94 application fee on any alien submitting that application, with fiscal 2025 minimum $24 or higher DHS rule amount, later July-to-July CPI-U increments rounded down to the nearest dollar and no waiver/reduction. Twenty percent of collected fees goes to the existing Land Border Inspection Fee Account pursuant to 1356(q)(2), available to CBP to retain and spend without further appropriation for I-94 processing; amounts not deposited there go to Treasury. The complete pre-vote subsection (q) establishes the account and its land-port receipt/expense/report framework. That baseline account scope is not substituted for the new section's any-alien I-94 application predicate, and its appropriations refunds are not applicant reimbursements. The visa fee and I-94 fee have separate collection events and dispositions; neither proves actual admission, visa compliance, a collection or immigration-status outcome. Senate 100014 amends the existing ESTA fee components under complete pre-vote1187(h)(3): the existing $17 per travel authorization remains, the separate full-System-cost-recovery component gains a $10 MINIMUM while retaining that cost condition, and a new component is at least $13 PER TRAVEL AUTHORIZATION. This does not describe a $10 or $13 total or first creation of ESTA. Its sunset edit extends the clause(i)(I) Travel Promotion Fund fee restriction from fiscal years beginning after October31,2028 to those beginning after October31,2034; it is not a sunset of every component. Its fiscal2026-onward CPI-U adjustment names the clause(i)(II) amount but literally uses the prior fee required UNDER THIS SUBPARAGRAPH as its base. That component/base relationship remains a separate application question, not a silently substituted isolated cost component or definite whole-fee adjustment; no increment-rounding rule is printed. Unlike selected House70017, this section does not edit existing clause(ii) disposition language: that baseline directs (i)(I) to the Travel Promotion Fund and (i)(II) to Treasury for System administration, but does not assign newly added (i)(III) by name. The new $13 component's disposition is separately reserved, without copying the House Treasury sentence or claiming to have closed other package funding provisions. Exact officialPDFpages819-821 visually confirm the printed adjustment language and section boundary; no HTML-parser repair is made. Existing travel-eligibility/admissibility/visa-eligibility distinctions remain, and no express new ESTA fee-waiver prohibition or inferred waiver availability is imported from EVUS. Senate 100015 separately adds an EVUS fee at enrollment for any alien SUBJECT to that System, additional to other authorized fees, with fiscal2025 minimum $30 or a higher DHS rule amount, later CPI-U increments rounded down to $0.25 and no waiver/reduction. It inserts a new1356(w) CBP EVUS Account with deposits equal to fees received MINUS $5 multiplied by the NUMBER OF PAYMENTS collected; that same $5-times-payments amount goes to Treasury. This payment-count language is retained rather than substituted with House70019's per-enrollment wording or inferred one-payment-per-enrollment implementation. Account amounts are appropriated without further appropriation and available until expended for CBP EVUS administration costs. OfficialPDF823 confirms the payment-count basis. The fee does not expand who is subject to EVUS, establish admission or visa/status eligibility, prove compliance or document an actual payment. Senate 100013 adds ten EOIR fee provisions despite its narrower adjustment-of-status section title. In(a), an alien who files the specified adjustment application with immigration court OR whose application is adjudicated there pays at filing OR before court adjudication. In(b)/(c), the fee is required from any alien at court filing of the inadmissibility-waiver/TPS application OR before court adjudication. No automatic duplicate charge at both events is asserted. The(d)/(e) alien appeals, (f) practitioner appeal and(g) alien motion collect at filing. The(h) suspension application and(i) application for an alien who is a lawful permanent resident collect at court filing. Senate(j) separately requires a payer who IS NOT A LAWFUL PERMANENT RESIDENT at the time that payer files with immigration court a cancellation/adjustment application FOR ANY ALIEN; this wording is not silently collapsed into House's application-category wording or an assumed identity of payer and beneficiary. The ten listed fiscal2025 floors are separate fee events, additional to other authorized fees, with a higher AttorneyGeneral rule amount permitted: adjustment to lawful permanent residence $1,500; waiver of grounds of inadmissibility $1,050; TPS $500; appeal from an immigration-judge decision $900; appeal from a DHS-officer decision $900; practitioner disciplinary appeal $1,325; motion to reopen or reconsider an immigration-judge or Board of Immigration Appeals decision $900; suspension of deportation application $600; cancellation of removal for the specified permanent-resident category $600; and cancellation/adjustment for the specified nonpermanent-resident category $1,500. Each subsection has fiscal2026-onward July-to-July CPI-U adjustment of its own prior-year fee, with the INCREMENT rounded down to $10, not an automatically exact future price or a sum charged to every alien. The disciplinary appeal payer is a PRACTITIONER filing an appeal of an adjudicating official's decision in a practitioner disciplinary case, not every alien or every attorney. The immigration-judge appeal provision separately excludes appeals of BOND decisions. The motion-fee exception identifies only motions to REOPEN an IN-ABSENTIA removal order under240(b)(5)(C)(ii) or an in-absentia deportation order under legacy242B(c)(3)(B), with the version's own printed temporal wording retained below. Complete pre-vote1229a(b)(5)(C)(ii) allows the identified motion at any time upon demonstrating either lack of notice in accordance with1229(a)(1) OR(a)(2), OR Federal/State custody AND nonappearance through no fault of the alien. Complete historical1252b(c)(3)(B) likewise allows the identified motion at any time upon demonstrating lack of notice in accordance with its(a)(2), OR Federal/State custody AND nonappearance through no fault of the alien. The surrounding notice/address requirements remain; these are not exemptions for every missed hearing, any custody, all reopening/reconsideration motions, or the separate180-day exceptional-circumstances grounds in240(b)(5)(C)(i)/242B(c)(3)(A). A fee exception does not establish that a motion was granted or an order actually rescinded. The1995Code historical section is corroborated by the later repeal/history notice and enacted104-208: its intervening371(b)(7) changes only242B(d)(1) officer terminology, not(c)(3)(B), and its309 effective-date/transition provisions remain qualified. Current repeal metadata is not substituted for operative legacy text. Senate(g)(3)(B) literally ends with a motion filed in accordance with242B(c)(3)(B) PRIOR TO APRIL1,1997, without House's explicit AS THE SECTION EXISTED phrase. The printed date attachment remains an application question: no definite pre1997 filing cutoff or deletion of the date is accepted, and the underlying legacy statute's at-any-time text remains visible. OfficialPDF812 visually confirms the same wording; it is not repaired as a parser error. Senate100013 prints NO express section-wide no-waiver/reduction clause; House(k) is not imported and availability of a waiver is not inferred. Every(a)-(j) disposition instead names fees collected pursuant to THIS SUBSECTION, with a not-more-than25percent ExaminationsFeeAccount transfer/EOIR retention-and-spending cap and amounts not transferred/credited toTreasury; Senate(a) does not copy House's50percent cap. These ceilings are not mandatory actual percentages, direct refunds to applicants or new account creation. Senate(k) bars EOIR expenditure of section-collected fees for the Legal Orientation Program OR any successor, without establishing termination or a universal funding ban. No component preference follows from either member's whole-package vote. Senate 10108 replaces SNAP2015(f) with its own exact individual-status list. The replacement is a NECESSARY individual-status condition for a member of an OTHERWISE ELIGIBLE household, not a sufficient promise of SNAP entitlement. US RESIDENCE is common to EACH of the four alternatives, AND the individual must meet at least one listed category: (A) a citizen OR NATIONAL of the UNITED STATES; (B) the defined lawful permanent-resident immigrant, retaining the express exclusion of ordinary temporary visitors/tourists/diplomats/students with no intention of abandoning foreign residence; (C) the version's own status category described below; OR (D) an individual lawfully residing in the US IN ACCORDANCE WITH a Compact of Free Association referred to in PRWORA402(b)(2)(G). Complete1101(a)(15)/(20)/(22) defines immigrant/nonimmigrant classes, unchanged lawful permanent residence and US national, without treating every lawful temporary stay or every foreign national as a listed status. Complete1612(b)(2)(G) identifies the US Compacts with the Federated States of Micronesia, Marshall Islands and Palau; nationality alone is not substituted for the proposal's lawful-residence-under-Compact condition. The complete pre-vote2015(f) already requires residence and lists citizen/LPR, the specified1259 deemed-permanent-residence category, conditional entry under1157/1158, the described1182(d)(5) parole and withholding under1231(b)(3). The amendment replaces that subsection's list: its old conditional-entry/general-parole/withholding categories are no longer separate entries, whereas defined permanent residence remains. The new text expressly says citizen OR USnational and supplies its own(C)/(D); it is not described as the first possible benefit for USnationals or COFA residents. Complete pre-vote1611/1612/1613/1641 separately retain qualified-alien definitions, program-specific restrictions/exceptions, the qualified-status five-year framework with its exceptions, and the2024COFA provisions. Qualification alone was not a complete entitlement, nor does the selected replacement directly amend every one of those separate laws. No blanket claim that every refugee, asylee, parolee or other national loses or gains benefits is made; another independently held listed status, other applicable rules and actual eligibility determination remain distinct. The replacement RETAINS consideration of the INELIGIBLE INDIVIDUAL'S income (less a pro-rata share AT STATE OPTION) AND financial resources when determining the eligibility and allotment value of that individual's household. The State-option modifier concerns the income pro-rata subtraction, not exclusion of all financial resources or automatic termination of all household members. The prior statutory paragraph already has this calculation language; it is not a new proof of spending, a specific household's benefit amount or a benefit award. Whole-package votes do not establish component preferences. Senate(C) instead identifies an alien who HAS BEEN GRANTED the status of Cuban and Haitian entrant AS DEFINED in501(e) ofPL96-422; it does not copy the House203(a)-petition/no-visa/physical-presence-in-specific-parole-program conjunction. The complete definition distinguishes(1) special Cuban/Haitian-entrant parole or subsequently established special immigration status, regardless of status WHEN ASSISTANCE/SERVICES ARE PROVIDED, from(2) OTHER Cuban/Haitian nationals who satisfy at least one of parole-with-no-other-acquired-INA-status, removal proceedings, or pending asylum application, AND have NO final,nonappealable,legally-enforceable removal order. The no-final-order predicate belongs to category(2), not silently to every category(1) case; no-other-acquired-status belongs to its own parole alternative. Printed HASBEENGRANTED wording remains, without treating nationality or the definition's service-time wording as proof of an actual grant or SNAP determination. Existing US-residence/otherwise-eligible-household and separate public-benefit rules remain common; this is not eligibility for every Cuban or Haitian national. Senate 71109 adds 1903(v)(5), beginning October 1, 2026: EXCEPT for existing (v)(2) emergency care and (v)(4) State-option assistance, payment to a State for medical assistance requires BOTH residence in one of the 50 States, the District of Columbia or a US territory AND at least ONE own listed status: US citizen OR US national; the defined lawful permanent-resident immigrant; an alien who HAS BEEN GRANTED defined Cuban and Haitian entrant status; OR lawful US residence IN ACCORDANCE WITH a referenced Compact of Free Association. Residence is COMMON TO EACH ordinary status alternative. The clause expressly excludes the described ordinary temporary visitors, tourists, diplomats and students from its permanent-resident alternative; neither any lawful temporary stay nor nationality alone is substituted for a listed status. This is a necessary federal State-payment condition, not sufficient individual eligibility or an award. The complete incorporated definitions preserve unchanged lawful permanent residence and US national meaning, the referenced Compacts and the distinct 501(e) entrant branches already source-bound in the SNAP component. Special entrant parole/subsequent special status retains its own service-time wording; OTHER Cuban/Haitian nationals require their own parole-with-no-other-acquired-INA-status OR removal-proceedings OR pending-asylum alternative AND no final, nonappealable, legally enforceable removal order. The no-order modifier is not transferred to every special-status case, and service-time wording does not prove the proposal's HAS BEEN GRANTED predicate. Complete pre-vote public-benefit restrictions and exceptions remain separate; the provision is not described as the first COFA framework or a categorical outcome for every refugee/asylee/parolee who may independently hold another listed status or qualify under an exception. The preserved (v)(2) exception requires ALL of emergency-treatment necessity, otherwise meeting State-plan eligibility with the named aid/SSI/supplement disregards, AND care not related to an organ transplant. The (v)(3) emergency definition includes emergency labor/delivery and the specified acute-severity/immediate-attention risk tests; it is not all medical care. Preserved (v)(4) is a STATE ELECTION for otherwise eligible LAWFULLY US-RESIDING children UNDER 21 and/or women in its printed pregnancy/60-day category, including its battered-individual reference, sponsor and ongoing lawful-residence verification rules. It is not automatic assistance for every child or pregnant person regardless of lawful residence, election or other eligibility. The printed (v)(4) category is not used to infer a universal postpartum cutoff or resolve every other coverage law. CHIP incorporates the new (v)(5) restriction EXCEPT in relation to payments for services under 2105(a)(1)(D)(ii), whose complete baseline concerns health-services initiatives to improve children's health, including targeted and other low-income children. This is not a pregnancy-only exception, every child's guaranteed coverage, or an exception for every CHIP expenditure. Complete 2107(e) and the expressly incorporated EAS71103(b) renumbering are bound before the further 71109(b) insertion; unrelated address/simultaneous-enrollment rules are not turned into immigration meanings. The section appropriates $15 million to CMS for fiscal 2026 implementation, available until expended, without establishing actual spending or benefit amounts. House section 44110's verification-period option and House section 44111's rate provision are not imported into this Senate clause. Senate section 71110 adds 1905(kk), beginning October 1, 2026: NOTWITHSTANDING (y) and (z), the matching percentage for payments for care/services described in 1903(v)(2), furnished to an alien described in 1903(v)(1), SHALL NOT EXCEED the percentage determined under 1905(b) FOR THAT STATE. It concerns that emergency-care payment category and its own described recipient, not every Medicaid service, an end to emergency eligibility or the House's specified-State 80-percent rule beginning a year later. Complete 1903(v)(2)/(3) retains emergency necessity AND otherwise State-plan eligibility with the named disregards AND no organ-transplant procedure, along with the printed emergency-condition definition. The reference to (v)(1) is retained rather than converted into an exhaustive immigration-status label. Complete pre-vote 1905(b)/(y)/(z) supplies the ordinary State percentage and enhanced expansion/early-expansion framework against which the cap is described. The (b) percentage is State-specific and includes its own statutory rules; no flat nationwide 50-percent cap, mandatory rate exactly equal to the ceiling or repeal of every other matching rule is inferred. The section also appropriates $1 million to CMS for fiscal year 2026 implementation, available until expended; this is an appropriation, not proven spending, a beneficiary payment or quantified savings. The earlier EAS section 71109 emergency exception is not erased by this matching-rate provision. Senate section 71201 proposes its own new Medicare status restriction and longer existing-enrollee transition. The new section 1899C makes a listed immigration/citizenship category NECESSARY for entitlement to or enrollment in Title XVIII benefits, subject to its own existing-enrollee transition; the list is not sufficient entitlement, an award or proof that a person satisfies all other Medicare requirements. It lists US citizen OR US national, lawful permanent residence under the INA, the version's own category(3), OR lawful US residence in accordance with a referenced Compact of Free Association. Unlike the new SNAP/Medicaid lists, 1899C(a) does not print a NEW COMMON RESIDENCE modifier across every alternative; the COFA alternative keeps its own lawful-residence predicate and other existing Medicare residence rules retain their own scopes. Complete material pre-vote 226/226A/1836 and 1818(a)/1818A(a) are bound. They distinguish hospital entitlement through the named age/insured-benefit, disability/railroad/government-employment or renal-disease pathways from separate Part B or premium Part A enrollment paths. In 1836(a), existing Part A entitlement is an ALTERNATIVE to the age 65/US-resident branch, whose citizen OR LPR alternatives have a five-year continuous-residence condition on the LPR branch. Complete 1818(a) has its own age 65, Part B enrollment, US residence, citizen OR LPR-with-five-years and no-other-Part-A-entitlement conjunction. The five-year modifier is not applied to every citizen, every enrollee or every entitlement path. The limited 1836(b) post-renal immunosuppressive-drug enrollment and own other-coverage exclusions remain distinct from full benefits. Complete 1818A(a) preserves its own disabled/earnings-related premium eligibility, not a generic disability guarantee. Neither age alone nor listed status alone is described as sufficient; the selected proposal does not directly rewrite each underlying benefit rule or establish an exhaustive pre-vote eligibility universe. The transition applies specifically to individuals ENTITLED TO OR ENROLLED FOR Title XVIII benefits AS OF ENACTMENT. The Commissioner must review that cohort to identify people not described in ANY of the four listed alternatives, and notify EACH identified person of termination at the enactment-relative date, as soon as practicable AFTER IDENTIFICATION and in a manner designed to ensure comprehension. The termination date is not measured from receipt or sending of the notice; the review deadline is not the termination date. No identical grace period is promised to every later applicant, perpetual grandfathering, actual completed review, actual termination or observed administrative outcome is inferred. Enactment-relative dates are not converted into dates based on this vote or the later enacted law. Senate category(3) instead requires an alien who HAS BEEN GRANTED Cuban and Haitian entrant status as defined in 501(e). The complete definition retains the special-parole/subsequent-special-status category's service-time wording, and the OTHER Cuban/Haitian-national category's (parole with NO other-acquired-INA-status OR removal proceedings OR pending asylum) AND NO final/nonappealable/legally-enforceable removal-order grouping. The no-order modifier stays in the latter category and the no-other-status modifier in its parole alternative; nationality or service-time wording does not prove an actual grant. House 203(a)-petition/visa/program predicates are not imported. (3) Safety and suitability assessments (A) In general Subject to the requirements of subparagraph (B), an unaccompanied alien child may not be placed with a person or entity unless the Secretary of Health and Human Services makes a determination that the proposed custodian is capable of providing for the child's physical and mental well-being. Senate own new 25F clause a: (a) Allowance of Credit.--In the case of an individual who is a citizen or resident of the United States (within the meaning of section 7701(a)(9)), there shall be allowed as a credit against the tax imposed by this chapter for the taxable year an amount equal to the aggregate amount of qualified contributions made by the taxpayer during the taxable year. Senate own new 25F clause b: (b) Limitations.-- (1) In general.--The credit allowed under subsection (a) to any taxpayer for any taxable year shall not exceed $1,700. (2) Reduction based on state credit.--The amount allowed as a credit under subsection (a) for a taxable year shall be reduced by the amount allowed as a credit on any State tax return of the taxpayer for qualified contributions made by the taxpayer during the taxable year. Senate own new 25F clause c: (c) Definitions.--For purposes of this section-- (1) Covered state.--The term `covered State' means one of the States, or the District of Columbia, that, for a calendar year, voluntarily elects to participate under this section and to identify scholarship granting organizations in the State, in accordance with subsection (g). (2) Eligible student.--The term `eligible student' means an individual who-- (A) is a member of a household with an income which, for the calendar year prior to the date of the application for a scholarship, is not greater than 300 percent of the area median gross income (as such term is used in section 42), and (B) is eligible to enroll in a public elementary or secondary school. (3) Qualified contribution.--The term `qualified contribution' means a charitable contribution of cash to a scholarship granting organization that uses the contribution to fund scholarships for eligible students solely within the State in which the organization is listed pursuant to subsection (g). (4) Qualified elementary or secondary education expense.--The term `qualified elementary or secondary education expense' means any expense of an eligible student which is described in section 530(b)(3)(A). (5) Scholarship granting organization.--The term `scholarship granting organization' means any organization-- (A) which-- (i) is described in section 501(c)(3) and exempt from tax under section 501(a), and (ii) is not a private foundation, (B) which prevents the co-mingling of qualified contributions with other amounts by maintaining one or more separate accounts exclusively for qualified contributions, (C) which satisfies the requirements of subsection (d), and (D) which is included on the list submitted for the applicable covered State under subsection (g) for the applicable year. Senate own new 25F clause d: (d) Requirements for Scholarship Granting Organizations.-- (1) In general.--An organization meets the requirements of this subsection if-- (A) such organization provides scholarships to 10 or more students who do not all attend the same school, (B) such organization spends not less than 90 percent of the income of the organization on scholarships for eligible students, (C) such organization does not provide scholarships for any expenses other than qualified elementary or secondary education expenses, (D) such organization provides a scholarship to eligible students with a priority for-- (i) students awarded a scholarship the previous school year, and (ii) after application of clause (i), any eligible students who have a sibling who was awarded a scholarship from such organization, (E) such organization does not earmark or set aside contributions for scholarships on behalf of any particular student, and (F) such organization-- (i) verifies the annual household income and family size of eligible students who apply for scholarships to ensure such students meet the requirement of subsection (c)(2)(A), and (ii) limits the awarding of scholarships to eligible students who are a member of a household for which the income does not exceed the amount established under subsection (c)(2)(A). (2) Prohibition on self-dealing.-- (A) In general.--A scholarship granting organization may not award a scholarship to any disqualified person. (B) Disqualified person.--For purposes of this paragraph, a disqualified person shall be determined pursuant to rules similar to the rules of section 4946. Senate own new 25F clause e: (e) Denial of Double Benefit.--Any qualified contribution for which a credit is allowed under this section shall not be taken into account as a charitable contribution for purposes of section 170. Senate own new 25F clause f: (f) Carryforward of Unused Credit.-- (1) In general.--If the credit allowable under subsection (a) for any taxable year exceeds the limitation imposed by section 26(a) for such taxable year reduced by the sum of the credits allowable under this subpart (other than this section, section 23, and section 25D), such excess shall be carried to the succeeding taxable year and added to the credit allowable under subsection (a) for such taxable year. (2) Limitation.--No credit may be carried forward under this subsection to any taxable year following the fifth taxable year after the taxable year in which the credit arose. For purposes of the preceding sentence, credits shall be treated as used on a first-in first-out basis. Senate own new 25F clause g: (g) State List of Scholarship Granting Organizations.-- (1) List.-- (A) In general.--Not later than January 1 of each calendar year (or, with respect to the first calendar year for which this section applies, as early as practicable), a State that voluntarily elects to participate under this section shall provide to the Secretary a list of the scholarship granting organizations that meet the requirements described in subsection (c)(5) and are located in the State. Senate own new 25F clause h: (h) Regulations and Guidance.--The Secretary shall issue such regulations or other guidance as the Secretary determines necessary to carry out the purposes of this section, including regulations or other guidance-- (1) providing for enforcement of the requirements under subsections (d) and (g), and (2) with respect to recordkeeping or information reporting for purposes of administering the requirements of this section.. ACA status treatment concerns a LAWFULLY PRESENT ALIEN who IS AND IS REASONABLY EXPECTED FOR THE ENTIRE CREDIT-ENROLLMENT PERIOD to hold an own listed LPR, version-specific Cuban-related or COFA status; these conditions are common to each alternative. Exchange verification concerns INDIVIDUAL CREDIT COVERAGE MONTHS, not an enrollment ban: failure of this paragraph ALONE does NOT make an individual ineligible to enroll. The qualifying child's defined SSN is required in either case. The Senate also requires the taxpayer's defined SSN or, on a joint return, the defined SSN of at least one spouse. Complete 24/152 retain own qualifying-child, NOT-ATTAINED-17, citizenship/residence/adoption, relationship/support/abode/joint-return/tie/custody and other exceptions, income/refundable/identification/year limits. Mathematical-error scope changes to SECTION 24; own alleged-error/explanation notice, no petition BASED ON THAT NOTICE, abatement request WITHIN 60 DAYS AFTER NOTICE SENT, mandatory abatement UPON RECEIPT, deficiency reassessment and collection stay remain. No actual fraud, debt, indexed payment, credit/refund, every-remedy loss or individual/tax-family determination.

The Senate $6,000 deduction is per qualified person. The listed alternatives are the taxpayer or the spouse on a joint return. In either case, the claimed person must have attained 65 before the tax year closes and must supply that person's defined SSN. One spouse's number does not establish deductions for both. The phaseout rate is 6 percent over $75,000, or $150,000 on a joint return. A taxpayer married within section 7703 must file jointly with the spouse; the new House similar-32(d) clause, blind bonus and hypothetical-itemizer mechanism are not imported. Own mathematical-error label is (W). The same-version SSN definition permits issuance to either a US citizen or the named work-authorized-alien category. In either case, the number must have been issued before the due date for the return. Other SSA numbers or ITINs do not alone qualify. Child-credit identification is not senior identification. Own taxable-income, itemization, spouse/exemption and marital predicates remain, along with the nonresident-alien standard-deduction exclusion, without an individual eligibility finding or accepted override. A deduction is not a dollar-for-dollar credit, exemption of all Social Security income or guaranteed refund. Both senior amendments apply to taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024; their own upper limit is a taxable year beginning before January 1, 2029. Modified income includes the named 911/931/933 exclusions. Mathematical-error notice requires the alleged error and explanation; the no-petition rule concerns that notice. The abatement request period is 60 days after notice is sent, abatement follows receipt, reassessment uses deficiency procedures and collection is stayed during the abatement period. No actual debt, fraud, payment or loss of every remedy.

Senate requires the individual's defined SSN in all cases. A credit for the qualified expenses of an individual other than the taxpayer or spouse must also include that individual's name and defined SSN. No new House spouse-number or similar-32(d) amendment is imported; retained 25A(g)(6) requires joint filing for a taxpayer married within 7703. No separate-return eligibility or child-credit joint-number alternative is inferred. The same-version defined SSN permits citizen issuance or the named work-authorized-alien branch. The institution EIN clause is AOTC-only and tied to the named taxpayer-paid qualified expenses taken into account, with retained dependent-payment treatment; it is not a Lifetime Learning or every-institution requirement. Full credit, income, student, institution, qualified-expense, assistance, dependent, prepayment, double-benefit, payee-statement, refund and recapture conditions remain, without an individual amount or eligibility determination. The AOTC student reference freezes HEA 484(a)(1), with its own exceptions, at August 5, 1997; it does not import all current student eligibility or its citizenship paragraph. The institution definition retains frozen HEA 481 and its own title IV eligibility condition. Exact historical passages and amendment chronology are bound; full HEA 481 comparison uses two declared split-word normalizations, without source mutation or personal/institution classification. A taxpayer nonresident during any portion of the year retains the conditional 6013(g)/(h) chapter-1 resident-election path, each with own spouse/status/both-election and duration/termination/re-election predicates; this is not all-noncitizen denial or immigration status/work authorization. Both apply to taxable years beginning after December 31, 2025. Own mathematical-error (J) changes TIN to SSN or EIN; alleged-error/explanation notice, 60 days after notice is sent, abatement upon receipt, deficiency reassessment and collection stay remain. No debt, wrongdoing, guaranteed credit/refund, loss of every remedy or whole-package closure.

No individual enforcement/child outcome, actual hire/award/data/reimbursement/expenditure or full-package closure.

Senate 100054(2)/(3) drug/prosecution purposes use the shared $3.33 billion fiscal year 2025 envelope through September 30, 2029, without House earmarks. Own listed matters include unlawful voting; full 611 federal-office/exception/nonapplication predicates remain, no generic alien-guilt or new benefit/voting rule. Separate 100055 DOJ Fund. The Attorney General shall use the Fund amounts for grants to eligible States, State agencies, and units of local government, pursuant to their existing statutory authorities, for any of the following purposes. The paragraph 1 purpose is locating and apprehending aliens who have committed a crime under Federal, State, or local law, in addition to being unlawfully present in the United States. The paragraph 2 purpose is collection and analysis of law enforcement investigative information within the United States to counter gang or other criminal activity. The paragraph 3 purpose is investigating and prosecuting crimes committed by aliens within the United States and drug and human trafficking crimes committed within the United States. The paragraph 4 purpose is court operations related to the prosecution of crimes committed by aliens and drug and human trafficking crimes. The paragraph 5 purpose is temporary criminal detention of aliens. The paragraph 6 purpose is transporting aliens described in paragraph (1) within the United States to locations related to the apprehension, detention, and prosecution of such aliens. The paragraph 7 purpose is vehicle maintenance, logistics, transportation, and other support provided to law enforcement agencies by a State agency to enhance the ability to locate and apprehend aliens who have committed crimes under Federal, State, or local law, in addition to being unlawfully present in the United States. Paragraphs (1) and (7) retain their own additional-crime and unlawful-presence requirements; paragraph (6) retains the paragraph (1) person category, its domestic transport limit and its destination purposes. Those requirements are not imported into the other purposes. Temporary criminal detention is distinct from civil immigration detention. Court paragraph (4) prints no separate within-the-United-States phrase; no neighboring location condition is borrowed. Listed conjunctions report the source categories, not a determination that a particular grant must fund both crime categories. Existing statutory authorities do not create new State arrest/removal powers or establish actual crime/status/expense eligibility. Fiscal year 2025 appropriation is not to exceed $3,500,000,000 ($3.5 billion) until September 30, 2028, with qualified and documented expenses. The Attorney General may provide grants to State agencies and units of local government for their expenditures for completed, ongoing, or new activities determined to be eligible for such grant funding that occurred on or after January 20, 2021. Amounts made available under this section shall be distributed to more than 1 State. No borrowed January 21 or 2029 date, automatic grant, actual crime/status/detention/hiring/spending or full-package closure. Existing question 46 subsection-scope application is unchanged.

Senate 100051(9)/(10) use the additional fiscal year 2025 $2,055,000,000 DHS envelope through September 30, 2029, in accordance with 235(b)(1)/(c), without House earmarks, House's express 212(a)(2)/(3) grounds wording or regardless-of-presence phrase. Senate 100051(8) and (11) are purposes within the additional $2,055,000,000 fiscal year 2025 appropriation to the Secretary of Homeland Security, available through September 30, 2029. Neither purpose is a separate earmark for the full account, the ICE account or a House child appropriation. Paragraph (8) funds removal operations for specified unaccompanied alien children, but amounts under this paragraph shall only be used for permitting a specified unaccompanied alien child to withdraw the application for admission of the child pursuant to section 235(a)(4). The Secretary of Homeland Security must determine on a case-by-case basis all three specified-child conditions. First, the child has been found by an immigration officer at a land border or port of entry of the United States and is inadmissible under the Immigration and Nationality Act. Second, the child has not been a victim of severe forms of trafficking in persons, and there is no credible evidence that such child is at risk of being trafficked upon return of the child to the child's country of nationality or country of last habitual residence. Third, the child does not have a fear of returning to the child's country of nationality or country of last habitual residence owing to a credible fear of persecution. The paragraph does not print the House express contiguous-or-non-contiguous-country phrase or an independent-decision finding; neither is silently inserted into its definition. The incorporated unaccompanied-alien-child definition requires no lawful immigration status in the United States and not having attained 18 years of age, together with either no parent or legal guardian in the United States or no parent or legal guardian in the United States available to provide care and physical custody. The complete severe-forms-of-trafficking definition is bound with its own sex-trafficking and labor-or-services alternatives, force/fraud/coercion and under-18 distinctions; no label alone determines a child's eligibility. Paragraph (11) funds criminal and gang checks of defined unaccompanied alien children who are 12 years of age and older, including the examination of such unaccompanied alien children for gang-related tattoos and other gang-related markings. It prints no separate encountered-by-CBP condition; the House 70116 encounter condition is not imported. Its age-12 floor belongs to this check purpose, not the paragraph (8) withdrawal definition. Examination funding is not a finding that a child belongs to a gang, has committed a crime or is dangerous. Complete material captured pre-vote 235(a)(4) retains discretionary permission to withdraw and depart immediately, not a mandatory withdrawal or removal order. Complete TVPRA 235/1232 retains its own contiguous-child case-by-case trafficking/fear and independent-decision conditions, discretionary withdrawal/return, safe-return conditions, 48-hour screening and failed-or-undetermined-screen transfer, other-child custody pathway and own notification/72-hour-transfer exceptions. Its removal-proceedings, relief/access-to-counsel, placement, suitability and remaining safeguards retain their own scope. Senate funding does not itself establish their repeal, fulfillment or a universal individual return, protection or counsel outcome. Exact application interaction remains separate question 49; House question 43 is preserved independently.

Senate 100051(5) fingerprint and DNA purposes are within the additional $2,055,000,000 fiscal year 2025 Secretary of Homeland Security account through September 30, 2029. Both purposes share the printed circumstance of aliens and alien children entering the United States without a valid visa. Subparagraph (A) funds collecting fingerprints, in accordance with section 262 and subsections (a)(3) and (b) of section 235 of the Immigration and Nationality Act. Subparagraph (B) separately funds collecting DNA, in accordance with sections 235(d) and 287(b) of that Act. These are funding purposes with their own incorporated authorities, not a determination that every alien or child is subject to every collection power or that funded collection actually occurred. Captured 262(a) concerns an alien now or hereafter in the United States who is fourteen years of age or older, has not been registered and fingerprinted under section 1201(b) or section 30 or 31 of the Alien Registration Act, 1940, and remains in the United States for thirty days or longer. All those conditions are common to its duty to apply for registration and to be fingerprinted before the expiration of such thirty days. Captured 262(b) separately requires a parent or legal guardian to apply for registration of an alien now or hereafter in the United States who is less than fourteen years of age, has not been registered under those named provisions, and remains in the United States for thirty days or longer, before that period expires. That parent/guardian provision prints registration, not the same under-14 fingerprint duty. Whenever an alien attains his fourteenth birthday in the United States, the separate rule requires in-person registration and fingerprinting within thirty days thereafter. Captured 262(c) retains the Attorney General's discretionary nonimmigrant fingerprint waiver on the basis of reciprocity pursuant to prescribed regulations; no actual waiver is inferred. Complete 235(a)(3) concerns inspection of aliens, including crewmen, who apply for or otherwise seek admission, readmission or transit; it does not itself print a fingerprint command. Complete material 235(b)(1)/(2) screening, exceptions, asylum/fear/interview/review/consultation/detention and contiguous-return conditions remain bound, together with the original favorable-admission challenge. January 29, 2025 Public Law 119-1 renumbers that original challenge from (3) to (4) and inserts the distinct State enforcement (3); the captured 2024 wording is not relabeled as an unamended 2025 subsection. Complete 235(d) retains its own belief-based conveyance search, detention/delivery with the alien-crewmember exception, named oath/evidence powers and subpoena-purpose/court-enforcement conditions. Complete 287(b) retains the designated officer/employee oath/evidence scope and its own knowing-or-willful false-evidence/perjury conditions. Neither cited provision expressly names DNA collection. That literal observation does not resolve whether other law, implementation rules or this funding language supports a proposed collection; question 50 reserves the exact DNA authority/application interaction.
